Narrator: Part two. You will hear someone giving a talk. For each question, fill in the missing information in the numbered space. Write one word or a number for each answer. You now have some time to look at questions.
Speaker 1: Welcome to today's lecture on Tashkent tours, a popular destination in Central Asia. Tashkent, the capital city of Uzbekistan, is known for its rich history, vibrant culture, and unique blend of ancient and modern attractions. Over the years, Tashkent has become a significant tourist hub, attracting visitors from around the world who want to explore its diverse offerings. Let's take a look at some of the key features that make Tashkent an exciting place for tourists.
Speaker 1: Firstly, Tashkent is famous for its ancient Islamic architecture, which reflects the region's long-standing cultural heritage. Tourists often visit the Khast Imam Complex, a historical and religious site that includes mosques, mausoleums, and libraries. This complex is particularly famous for housing one of the oldest copies of the Quran in the world, believed to date back to the seventh century. Another popular attraction in Tashkent is the Chorsu Bazaar. This vibrant market is a must-see for visitors, offering a variety of local goods, from spices to handicrafts. The bazaar is also a great place for tourists to sample traditional Uzbek foods, such as plov, a rice dish with meat, vegetables, and spices that is considered the national dish of Uzbekistan. For those interested in modern attractions, Tashkent has plenty to offer as well. The Tashkent TV Tower, standing at 375 meters, is one of the tallest towers in Central Asia. It has an observation deck that provides panoramic views of the city, giving tourists a unique perspective on the urban landscape. Visitors can also explore the Amir Timur Museum, dedicated to the historical figure Amir Timur, a Central Asian conqueror who played a significant role in the region's history. To help tourists explore these attractions, Tashkent offers various types of tours, including guided city tours, cultural tours, and food tours. There are even day trips that take visitors to nearby historical cities, such as Samarkand and Bukhara, which are part of the ancient Silk Road and offer additional insights into the region's rich history. In summary, Tashkent's unique combination of ancient landmarks and modern attractions, along with its strategic location on the Silk Road, makes it a fascinating destination for tourists from around the world.

parts.transcript:
Narrator: Part three. You will hear people speaking in different situations. Match each speaker, 15 to 18, to the options, A-F. There are two extra options which you do not need to use. Mark your answers on the answer sheet. You now have some time to look at questions.
Speaker 1: In our center, we offer lots of different courses and to all ages. It's a lot of fun when we have the hall packed with people. Every Wednesday and Friday, there are classes of ballroom and traditional dance. The look on the people's faces tells you everything you need to know. Everyone always seems to be enjoying themselves and having a great time. We get great crowds and it really gives a good sense of liveliness to the place. Mostly we get parents and people of that age, but we'd like to start classes aimed more specifically at young people. So far, we haven't been able to decide what kind of dance classes we should try and arrange. And also, we'd like to see more boys come, but finding one that all young teens will enjoy is not easy.
Speaker 2: In recent years, the unemployment levels have been quietly rising and it's on the jobs front where the effects are starting to be seen. We are partly government-funded organization and as much as possible operated by the local community for the local community. Job preparation and job assistance training are the primary services we provide. Of late, we've been running several language classes every other evening. On average, half of those who do sign up for our classes do so with the intention of emigrating. So, although we may lose people from the area, at the very least, the chances of them gaining employment and re-entering the workforce will be substantially increased.
Speaker 3: Our group runs in conjunction with the local council, and we generally maintain contact with the local schools. That's how we came to run after-school programs. There's no real structure to it as such, but we have an area for them to work on any school work or projects. We have a few computers, a pool table, which is free to anyone. We always have a trained teacher on staff, but that's more for the younger kids. We don't have daycare because that would be stretching ourselves a little too thin. But children from early primary education come in for a few hours after their school finishes, usually to wait for an older sibling to pick them up. I know it helps out the parents a lot. Normally school finishes a few hours before the parents finish work. So knowing their kids have a place to go where they're monitored gives them great peace of mind. It works for the children too, as they're being looked after and not being babysat.
Speaker 4: Local pride is something that shouldn't be taken lightly, and it's an easy thing to miss. I suppose I feel it more now that I'm in my 50s because it's certainly nothing I noticed as a youngster. I came to town several years ago and became involved in a tidy towns project. We take volunteers, but there is a core group of around 20 who go around the town and, for example, if there is an area of public land that is not well attended to, we may try and spruce it up. We've managed to convince the local council to allow us to convert one or two small pieces of land around the area so that they can be used as a place for recreation for families or visitors. We'd like to get control of one or two unused buildings and convert them so they could become of use to the community.

Narrator: You will hear a history student called Kylie giving a presentation to her class about an archaeological site in Egypt called Beni Hasan.
Speaker 1: I'm going to tell you about an archaeological site called Beni Hasan. It's located on the east bank of the Nile in central Egypt and it dates back to the 11th and 12th dynasties of Egypt's Middle Kingdom. That's 2050 to 1650 BCE.
Speaker 1: The site and its decorated tombs not only tell us about the artists who worked on the tombs, but also reflect the lives of the people buried there. The tombs that interest me most are those of government officials. Their servants wouldn't have had such elaborate tombs.
